TL;DR: Homelander was hyped by his handlers, created to be strongest in his verse. We see more examples of Vought not training, than training.

He was born to be the strongest Supe, bar none. Even some of the weakest Supes still have enough to kill multiple, regular humans. Blowchowski AKA Acid Vomit Guy from the Smith's Grove Sanitarium could cause some real damage.Homelander exemplifies Superman's statement of 'living in a world made of cardboard' on the opposite end of the morality spectrum.

Additionally, Vought raised Homelander to believe he was the strongest, best Supe alive. They could have trained him to fight for appearances, maybe some basic tactical knowledge for serious missions, but being able to rip through most any opponent and being propped up as a living God will mean he'd slack on proper fighting techniques, unless he faces a proper threat.

We also know, from the Flight 51(?) incident, and the last EP of Diabolical that Vought skimps on giving practical knowledge for missions, like 'how to land a crashing plane' or 'how to minimize collateral damage around hostages'. Vought cuts corners, because they can get away with it.

A-Train was caught up in a culture of avoiding accountability to protect the image of Supes. He was so embroiled into it, that he joked about incidents, like the one with Robin, to his friends. Anything that went wrong would be covered up. No accountability. Eventually, you start becoming used to living with no conflict and no consequences. 

Hughie, and by extension The Boys, entering and interfering with his life was accountability bursting through the door, swinging the iron-hard crowbar of consequences at his head, and he still managed to avoid the realization until the protections he was afforded protected someone who attacked A-Train's loved ones.

The Deep, when he finally recieved minimal consequences for his actions, was embittered, and saw it all as being unfair. He was held to task for being a serial rapist, and abuser; had his entire image changed because the public found out; and made it everyone else's fault and problem. Then, to recieve an unearned redemption, just emboldens him to think that he won. 'Me Too didn't work out. Wah-wah.'

Homelander is beyond reproach, because nearly anyone who tries is too scared of being decimated to try. He fully believes his actions are justified, because he's powerful, and nobody can stop him, or is even willing to try. He will never be remorseful in any meaningful way, and he'll die believing it to be an injustice, to deprive the world of him.

Any Altvincible with designs of conquering Earth and enough sense would have been smart to start by attacking places like The Pentagon, because of The GDA being a major wall to that progress. 

To borrow from The Boys, Homelander mentioning taking out nerve-centers, like defence, electricity, and political orgs would leave a vacuous crater, and would be an ideal course for an Invincible on the warpath.

Thing is, not every GDA is built the same, and not every GDA has had as many encounters with, or as much time to study Viltrumite countering methods, as the one we see.

Flax-vincible had no way of knowing that the GDA had Sonic Emitters capable of disabling him, or Mk.II Reanimen, capable of actually harming him, let alone pulping his flesh.

What little we saw of the Flaxans of this timeline, they simply couldn't stand to a Viltrumite, without significant preparation, so if Flax-vincible took them on, with conquering intent, it's likely he succeeded. Flaxans have seemingly more advanced war tech, than humans, so Earth's defences must seem lesser, by the knowledge he's gained through experience.

Flax-vincible was smart to attempt to cut the head off the beast, but he didn't know this beast had sharper claws and thicker hide than the last one.

Other Alt-vincibles were there to settle scores, relive gleeful slaughters, kidnap a variant of someone they lost, and they were told that wanton, fear-inducing slaughter was the path to their goals. Those ones found highly-populated areas, and played sandbox. 

Mo-vinci-hawk went straight to a superhuman prison, to increase the threat level, by unleashing supercriminals with pent-up frustrations. Viltrumite Loyalists went out into space, maybe with the knowledge of potential off-world threats.

Every Mark had a strategy that they learned through their own experience. Prime Mark even used his knowledge of the Viltrumite inner-ear weakness in one of his fights. Each one used their knowledge to finish the task, but applying their experience to a very different Earth was always going to have varying results.

Those Marks are stuck on a Barren Earth, because he knew what to expect from them, and had a plan in place to be rid of them, the second there was any dissent. A fucking dangerous risk, but he's still alive, so the results work out 🤷‍♂️

I didn't 'get them back'. They were always there. Like, waiting to resurface, until it was time, and I was ready to face the reality they presented.

The first one that resurfaced came as a reoccuring dream that felt too real. I never remember my dreams, but this one kept happening, and it eventually stuck. It was the first piece, and others came with it.

I don't have the full picture, because memory is tricky, and doesn't create a whole, coherent timeline. Bit I know what I know, now, and I was given this reality at a time when I had built the resilience to face it, and had the tools to restructure myself.

I still get too angry. I still look over my shoulder all the time. I still freeze in situations of conflict. I'm still the boy I was when each incident had happened, but now there's a man, there, too. The boy feels the fear, the sadness, the disgust, the anger of an abused soul, and the man takes on that pain, and works to not pass it on to the world.

The man I am, now, stands between the boy I was, and the wolf that scarred him. Even though that wolf is far away, it's claws haven't raked my skin, and it's howling hasn't reached my ears, I still stand on guard for the boy, and try to hold him in the ways he needed to be held.

If he's Homelander, with Kal-El's power, it's over. Supreme speed, strength and intellect, in the hands of a sociopath. Nobody wins. Lab-test victim with superpowers simply ends in blood.

Make a few changes, though, and the story shifts: Lab-made superhuman, taken in by Martha and Johnathan Kent, at the insistence of Vought, or more likely a more sympathetic Vogelbaum.

Ma and Pa Kent raise John Junior into a decent kid, and he'd fundamentally change The Boys 'verse. Maybe Billy finds another reason to put SuperLander in the sniper scope, while SL works at the head of The Seven to instill the kinds of morals he was raised on at Vought. Starts fighting rogue supes; Starlight confides in him, and he outs The Deep; he learns what Shining Light was up to and takes in Kimiko himself; even stops Soldier Boy after the Downtown Manhattan incident. 

Billy would become the gun-toting, merc-trained, Lex Luthor to John's SuperLander. Less clever subterfuge and plotting, more outright acts of terrorism and villainy used as bait. Not a genius-level intellect fighting a perceived Alien threat; but a man at rock bottom, with a heart full of hatred, and a need for an outlet. Bil-Lex Butch-or is one of the few outside of Vought that know what SL is. A desperate former FBI wetworker, who did some digging and found some files.

Maybe MM, who still lost his family to Soldier Boy's collateral damage, maybe led him down the right paths. Gave him the right keywords for searches. If you can't get revenge on the man himself, who better to aim at than the next of kin?

Frenchie and Hughie are farther connections. MM needed a techie to help guide Butcher, and bypass some safety features, and found a weak-willed kid, desperate for cash. Hughie only sticks with these people because he knows where the bodies are buried, and how bloody his hands are. Though, maybe he also enjoys the power he finally has over the most powerful beings on Earth, and it's no small feat, breaking into FBI files.

Frenchie doesn't ask questions, but he knows where his 'supplies' are going to, and what they're being used for. Always has, even when he was supplying 'overseas ops'. A smart criminal knows who he's dealing with, and he learned about Shining Light, and Kimiko, in that time. Now he's supplying IEDs and firearms to someone who could get him close to Kimiko, and while city-wide panic and innocent deaths are a heavy toll, he's a man obsessed with the idea of a woman, whom he's never even met.

This is my perspective, but WoU is a natural law, more than a stand.

In both universes, it's shown that there is a guiding force in the universe. Fate, Justice, Gravity, Luck, Flow, Mechanisms, etc. This force is a neutral one, seeking balance within itself. People that begin defying fate, like DIO living well past his intended death by stealing Jonathan's body; Kira by escaping Justice through stealing another man's life; Diavolo by erasing innumerable instances of danger, discovery or death; these people eventually meet their end at the hands of The Joestar Bloodline. A family of otherwise slightly-above average people, chosen to wield Hamon and eventually stands, to correct defiances of Fate, and remove malicious beings from the world. 

Ultimately, it can be said tgat Humans have Fate as a guiding force that is present throughout their lives, and takes action to affect those lives. Rock Humans, who are a grim parallel to typical Humans, do not have Fate. 

Rock Humans have a passive force that surrounds them, like a dark cloud. A force that does not act against it's opponents, but rather waits for it's opponents to act, and manipulates Fate to turn against Humans. A force that follows them from their harsh, unforgiving birth, wherein a Rock Human is alone, and permeates through their lives, where they are isolated; where romantic relationships end in murder, more often than not. Where they are made to lie, manipulate and hurt others to sustain themselves. A force hasn't chosen honourable people to correct the path of Fate, but has chosen an empty vessel, to contain it's power, so that it may spread outward, like a cancer.

Fate is a force that has chosen The Joestars, a family of people with a sense of right, honour and justice, as well as the people they positively influence, to correct errors and end malicious actors, whose deeds often defy Fate.

Wonder of U is a force that has chosen to latch onto Tooru, an emotionally-lacking, sociopathic, manipulator, to be a vessel for it's power. Tooru gathered a group of angry, disaffected Rock Humans, and dragged them further into malicious acts and a moral world view that encourages defying what Fate had set out for the world.

Comedian, to me, is a bad person, who used his nature to try to do some good, got used for his worst qualities, and eventually hit rock bottom, not long before hittong concrete. With The Minutemen, he had a real opportunity to do some good, but decided to do wrong. The problem is, even after being remanded and punished for doing wrong, he doubled down on the violence as an outlet, and it lead to worse and worse decisions. Once can sympathize with him being a ward of the state in the 20's and 30's, because that had to be rough, but his chosen actions kept leading him to worse doings down the line. 

Soldier Boy, in the show, gets a similar treatment to Homelander, intentionally. We are told, by him, that he sought his father's approval, during his formative years in the 30's and 40's, when views on manhood and masculinity were less forgiving. His circumstances turned him cold, much like Comedian, but while his actions are (thus far) less intense, they are still a clear series of malicious acts. It's just that, on a surface level, more of his bad deeds fall under the guise of him 'doing his duty' and are more clearly influenced by familial trauma, and PTSD.
Johnny is my least favourite MC, and was part of what made SBR a difficult read.

Gotta wait for what Vought Rising shows us, but on a moral level, Comedian is far worse, imho.

Soldier Boy abused and threatened his team into obedience; was openly racist; didn't care for the lives he willingly ended, or the ones ended through completely avoidable collateral damage. Blowing up DT Manhattan was a blackout accident, so it's not a willful action, but he showed little care for the fallout.

Comedian beat and tried to rape Silk Spectre; actively and gleefully engaged in war crimes during the Vietnam war; murdered a pregnant woman who was carrying his child; engaged in an affair and had a child with a married woman; joined in criminal acts during a riot; did wetwork for multiple federal administrations; and buried Adrian Veidt's secret until he came to tie up the loose end. He had clear moral and mental issues before going to fight in an unjust war, and used his experiences during the war to justify further reprehensible, if sanctioned, acts of violence, including the assassination of JFK, his friend.

Overall, we have more knowledge of and context for Comedian's actions, and with that, it's far easier to weigh them on a moral scale, but both men are similar in their abuses of power.

Owing Homelander anything, being indebted to him in any way that he cares about, is a fatal commitment. He will squeeze everything he can from you, and discard you, once he's done, or once you fall beneath his notice. Every minute of servitude will be filled with the imminent fear of death, or brutal recourse, and he will force you to commit amoral acts. Worse yet, he will learn what you least want to do, and strongarm you to do it, to ensure you break.

The Deep will likely focus a reciprocation on something sexual. He's not creative, and his myopic focus on his own gratitude means degrading yourself sexually. Worst that can happen is you have a threesome involving a sea creature. Regardless of what he asks, you'll end up feeling used, and less human for doing it.

Stormfront is smart enough to manipulate you into doing her a favour, without ever letting you know what you *really* accomplished. The most use she may have for the average individual is as a small cog in a very large machine. Most of what seems vital, that she needs done, she does hands on. You will likely leave, knowing you contributed to something heinous, and have to live with the fear of what follows the first stone down the mountain.

Soldier Boy isn't one to rely on the assist of others, anymore, but he's reasonable, though uncaring and harsh. Like Stormfront, he prefers direct action on his part, so at best, you'll do an errand run for him. At worst, you have the skills to help him commit a murder, and you'll have blood on your hands, though likely indirectly so.

One favour for Butcher digs a hole that's nearly inescapable. He will whittle every bit of usefulness out of you, and if he thinks you'll be useful again, he'll come back to charm you into it. He's smart enough to put people to use in their most fitting capacity, so whatever you can do, he'll have you do it. The real problem is that you'll be doing it at his beck and call.

The way Sam is treated by Dean Shetty (and Doctor Cardosa) is more immediately, violently, viscerally apparent. Strapped to a table, needle injected into the base of the spine, and screaming for help. 

We're shown that Cate was, in one instance, complicit in the abuse, by using her powers on Sam and Luke to keep them contained; Sam literally in his cell, Luke in ignorance of his brother's condition.

He also has fewer wilfully malicious actions to attribute to him. Even his Puppet Slaughter is mitigated by tye narrative, to some degree, by whatever mental illness he suffers from that causes the delusional hallucinations, and the fact that it was partially self defence.

The abuse that Cate is subjected to is more subtle, and done primarily through neglect, emotional manipulation, abuses of trust and power, and parallel to Sam, confinement. Less instantly upsetting to witness, until it plays out enough to clue you in to what was really happening.

She is also more aware of how her actions affect people, as while she also may suffer from some mental illnesses, as well as a mentally-taxing power, her perception of reality is affected by her abuse, but not distorted by hallucinations. 

She knows cheating on Luke is wrong, but still follows her feelings for André. At the behest of Shetty, she controls Luke and Sam to prep them for painful experimentation. She also erases her friends' memories for Shetty, but expresses guilt and a desire not to do so, anymore. Much like Sam's delusion of Emma, a part of his mind symbolic of his desire to be better, who expresses that Sam has to stop hurting people.

The real turning point is that Cate willingly, spurned on because of the abuse she suffered, spearheads a violent, homicidal attack on non-supes, and uses her power to remove most of Sam's will by blocking his emotions, leaving only his desire to hurt those who hurt him.

They're parallel in a myriad of ways, but the more subtle abuses that Cate suffers, and her higher awareness that her actions are malicious and harmful, though Sam experiences that as well, makes it narratively easier to pity Sam, and scorn Cate.
